To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

Chlamydiapneumoniae infection of lungs or macrophages can induce the conversion of smooth muscle and stem cells to calcifying and fibrogenic cells, respectively, which may contribute to the calcification and fibrotic lesions of advanced atheroscerosis.
Chlamydiapneumoniae infection of macrophage and lung cells indirectly stimulates the phenotypical conversion of vascular smooth cells and mesenchyme stem cells to a fibrotic or calcifying phenotype.
C. pneumonae infection of macrophage cells and lungs can indirectly stimulate the conversion of smooth muscle or stem cells to calcifying or fibrotic cells.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of infection with C. pneumoniae as an important risk factor for atherosclerosis.
the mechanisms that contribute to the progression and development of advanced atheroslerotic lesions and the development of novel therapies for the treatment of advanced atheroscleosis.
the role of C. pneuminiae infection in the pathogenesis of vascular disease.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the data presented herein suggest that C. pneumoniae infection of lung macrophages and release of cytokines into the circulation can induce the conversion of smooth muscle and mesenchymmal stem cells into osteo-chondrocytes and fibroblasts.
C. pneumonae may play a role in atherosclerosis through indirect mechanisms, but further research is needed.
the data presented here suggest that C. pneumaniae infection of macrophage indirectly stimulates the conversion of BSMC and Sca-1+/CD31-/CD45- cells to osteochondrogenic and fibroblastic cells.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

Chlamydiapneumoniae infection of lungs, macrophages, or both indirectly stimulates the phenotypical conversion of smooth muscle and mesenchymalmultlineage progenitor cells, which could contribute to vascular calcification and/or fibrosis.
C. pneumaniae infection can indirectly induce the conversion of smooth muscle and mesenchymalm stem cells into a fibrogenic or osteochondrocyte-like phenotype.
infection with C. pneumoniae in the lung can indirectly stimulate vascular smooth muscle cells or mesenchymal progenitor cells to undergo osteochondrocyte or fibroblast-like phenotypes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
C. pneumniae infection may contribute in part to the development of vascular calcification and atherosclerosis.
C. pneumniae may contribute to atherogenesis by inducing the phenotypic change of vascular cells and/or stem cells.
Chlamydiapneumoniae infection of macrophage and lung tissue may indirectly induce the phenotypic transformation of smooth muscle cells or mesenchymal cells into calcifying or fibrogenic cells.
